literal: Being deaf, he usually had nothing required of him; once he took to drink he would stay drunk for eight days.
idiomatic: Deaf as he was, he was left largely alone; a single bout of drinking could last eight days.

literal: The Duke of Yue, Yang Su, was then at the height of favor; he valued Biao's family standing and had his daughter marry Biao's son Xuanzong, with a bride-price very generous indeed.
idiomatic: Yang Su, Duke of Yue, then stood at the summit of imperial favor; he prized Biao's pedigree and married his daughter to Biao's son Xuanzong with lavish betrothal gifts.

literal: At the start of the wedding procession the hall was full of dukes and ministers; Su ordered them to ride out and meet the groom.
idiomatic: When the groom was to be escorted home, the seats were packed with nobles; Su sent them out on horseback to receive him.

literal: Biao came in worn cap and robes, riding a donkey.
idiomatic: Biao arrived in shabby dress, on a donkey.

literal: Su pushed him to the seat of honor; Biao's courtesy was very arrogant and his words insolent; Su angrily brushed his robe and rose, and the feast was broken up.
idiomatic: Su pressed him to the place of honor, but Biao was haughty in ritual and rude in speech; Su flung his sleeve and left, and the banquet ended in ruin.

literal: Several days later Biao came to apologize; Su treated him as before.
idiomatic: Days later Biao came to make amends; Su received him as though nothing had happened.

literal: An edict appointed him Governor of Yizhou; someone said he was unfit, and the appointment was recalled.
idiomatic: He was ordered to be Governor of Yizhou, but when some said he was not suited to the post the appointment was halted.

literal: Biao told people, "Why must the Governor of Yizhou surpass Dao Yi?"
idiomatic: Biao said to others, "Why should a Governor of Yizhou have to outshine Dao Yi?"

literal: In the Renshou era he died in the capital.
idiomatic: He died in the capital during Renshou.

literal: His son Shiji.
idiomatic: His son was Shiji.

literal: Zhongwen's younger brother Shuren was light and chivalrous and set great store by pledged friendship.
idiomatic: Zhongwen's younger brother Shuren was a swaggering knight who honored sworn bonds.

literal: He served Wei as Governor of Ying.
idiomatic: In Wei he became Governor of Ying.

literal: For corruption he was impeached by Censor-in-chief Gao Zhongmi and ordered to die at home.
idiomatic: Gao Zhongmi, Censor-in-chief, impeached him for graft and he was granted death in his own house.

literal: Facing execution he composed five quatrains to take leave of his brothers.
idiomatic: At the block he wrote five quatrains bidding his brothers farewell.

literal: He did not reach his brother Yan—because Yan had not exerted himself much to save him.
idiomatic: He never saw his brother Yan again—Yan, he felt, had not tried hard enough to rescue him.

literal: His son Yanwu had judgment and ability.
idiomatic: His son Yanwu was a man of insight and capacity.

literal: At the opening of Sui's Kaihuang he held the post of Governor of Wei.
idiomatic: In the first years of Sui's Kaihuang he was Governor of Wei.

literal: Shuren's younger brother Shuyi, in Emperor Xiaozhuang's time, was Director of the Storehouse in the Ministry.
idiomatic: Shuren's younger brother Shuyi, under Emperor Xiaozhuang of Wei, was Director of the Storehouse in the Ministry.

literal: At first Shuyi's father Xiu, as Governor of Qing, had released a bandit chieftain and ordered him to bring out his gang, and thus made them household retainers.
idiomatic: Earlier, when Shuyi's father Xiu was Governor of Qing, he freed a bandit leader and had him deliver his band—men Xiu then kept as retainers.

literal: In Luoyang he and his elder brother Shuren cast coin.
idiomatic: In Luoyang he and his elder brother Shuren counterfeited coin.

literal: When the affair came to light the whole family fled; Shuyi was seized.
idiomatic: When the crime was exposed the household fled together, but Shuyi was caught.

literal: The Prince of Chengyang, Hui, was Governor of Si; the Prince of Huaihuai, Yu, because the guilt was not Shuyi's own person, urgently spoke on his behalf.
idiomatic: Prince of Chengyang Hui held Si Province; Prince of Huaihuai Yu, holding that the fault was not Shuyi's alone, pleaded for him at once.

literal: Hui, because a marriage proposal had been refused, then withheld the pardon and had him executed.
idiomatic: Hui, whose offer of marriage had been spurned, held back the amnesty and put him to death.

literal: Shuyi's nephew's son Kan, by a false name, followed the army and stole rank as an officer of the Palace Secretariat.
idiomatic: Shuyi's nephew's son Kan enlisted under a borrowed name and by fraud won a post in the Palace Secretariat.

literal: He was impeached by Left Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing He Ziyue and lost his office.
idiomatic: He Ziyue, Left Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing, impeached him and he was dismissed.

literal: By nature he was also given to bravado.
idiomatic: He was swaggering by temperament as well.

literal: From then on he reformed himself, shut his door and read books, and at the time was called broadly learned.
idiomatic: He afterward mended his ways, closed his doors to study, and men of the day called him encyclopedic.

literal: Later he was also Token Attendant Cavalier and envoy to Liang, serving as Yang Fei's deputy.
idiomatic: He later served as Token Attendant Cavalier on a mission to Liang, as deputy to Yang Fei.

literal: Ashamed to rank below Fei and arrogant of his talent and standing, he called Fei "Master Yang," and his words always cut him down.
idiomatic: Loath to stand beneath Fei and proud of his own gifts and pedigree, he called Fei "Master Yang" and needled him at every turn.

literal: On his return he died on the road.
idiomatic: He died on the homeward journey.

literal: His son Zheng held the posts of Palace Steward and Governor of Wude commandery.
idiomatic: His son Zheng was Palace Steward and Governor of Wude.

literal: Kan's brother's son Zhi was Aide of Jizhou.
idiomatic: Kan's brother's son Zhi was Aide of Jizhou.

literal: Galloping in the chase, his hair caught in a tree and he died.
idiomatic: Riding hard after game, his hair caught in a branch and he was killed.

literal: His son Gui.
idiomatic: His son was Gui.

literal: Zhi's brother's son Yu was Governor of Dongguan.
idiomatic: Zhi's brother's son Yu was Governor of Dongguan.

literal: Yu's brother's son Yue.
idiomatic: Yu's brother's son was Yue.

literal: At five he lost his father and would not eat meat.
idiomatic: He lost his father at five and refused meat thereafter.

literal: Later, when his mother died, his mourning wore him to the bone.
idiomatic: When his mother died later, grief left him skin on bone.

literal: People said, "Cui Nine plays at filial piety—wind blows and he topples."
idiomatic: People said, "Cui Nine performs filial piety: a gust of wind and he falls over."

literal: After the month of mourning ended, his elder brother's son Du died, and for another hundred days he did not enter his chamber.
idiomatic: When the mourning month ended his elder brother's son Du died, and for another hundred days he would not go indoors.

literal: Over eight feet tall, with a bearing handsome and strange; he once watched the Liang envoy Liu Xiaoyi in secret, and those among the guests who saw him were startled.
idiomatic: He stood more than eight feet, his presence striking and otherworldly; he once stole a look at the Liang envoy Liu Xiaoyi, and even the retinue who noticed were shaken.

literal: In the Wuding era he was Sacrifice Wine on the staff of the Prince of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: Under Wuding he was Sacrifice Wine on the Prince of Pingyuan's staff.

literal: He and his elder brother's son Zhan both went to Jinyang and lodged in a Buddhist monastery.
idiomatic: He and his elder brother's son Zhan went together to Jinyang and stayed in a temple.

literal: Zhan was two years older than Yue; after court each would stand long while the other leaned on an armrest facing him—both splendid in bearing, like paired reflections.
idiomatic: Zhan was two years Yue's senior; after audience they would stand facing each other, one leaning on a couch—both radiant, like mirrors of one another.

literal: The monks peeked at them and thought them two beings from heaven.
idiomatic: Monks who spied on them whispered that two immortals had descended.

literal: In the Qianming era he was Director of Merit.
idiomatic: In Qianming he was Director of Merit.

literal: Sick and near death, he told Zhan, "Since the brothers died the house line has declined; at home there are only you and me."
idiomatic: Ill and dying, he said to Zhan, "Since our kinsmen died the line has crumbled; in this house only you and I remain."

literal: "Whether life is long or short—how is that worth grief?"
idiomatic: "Life's span—what is there to mourn?"

literal: "If you can escape this fate, I shall not die hungry."
idiomatic: "If you can survive what comes, I will not starve in the grave."

literal: Xiu's younger brother Yin, courtesy name Jingli, was Attendant of the Heir Apparent.
idiomatic: Xiu's younger brother Yin, style Jingli, was Attendant of the Heir Apparent.

literal: He died and was posthumously made Governor of Le'an.
idiomatic: When he died he was posthumously made Governor of Le'an.

literal: His wife was Princess Jinning, eldest daughter of the Prince of Le'an—chaste and of fine conduct.
idiomatic: His wife was Princess Jinning, eldest daughter of the Prince of Le'an, famed for steadfast virtue.

literal: His son Min, courtesy name Changqian, was clever in boyhood.
idiomatic: His son Min, style Changqian, was precocious as a child.

literal: The Governor of Jizhou, Lu Shangzhi, wished to give his eldest daughter to him; Yan sought Shangzhi's second daughter for Changqian, saying, "A household's way is ruled largely by its women; I wish the sisters to be sisters-in-law."
idiomatic: Lu Shangzhi, Governor of Jizhou, meant to marry his eldest daughter to him; Yan asked instead for Shangzhi's second daughter for Changqian, saying, "A house turns on its women—I want the girls to be sisters-in-law."

literal: Shangzhi was moved by the righteousness of it, and on the same day the weddings were held.
idiomatic: Moved by the sentiment, Shangzhi married both daughters on the same day.

literal: Xiu warned his sons, "You should all be one body; do not act as though you were only cousins under one roof."
idiomatic: Xiu admonished his sons, "Be one kin, not merely cousins sharing a hall."

literal: "If you do not heed my words, the spirits will not accept your sacrifices."
idiomatic: "Ignore me, and the ancestors will refuse your offerings."

literal: When Xiu died, writings were found in his pillow like the admonitions he had given in life, and the sons obeyed them.
idiomatic: After Xiu's death a text was found in his pillow, word for word his living counsel, and the sons followed it.

literal: Changqian and Xiu's second son Zhongwen were born in the same year, but Changqian was older by a month; the family called them Big Two and Little Two.
idiomatic: Changqian and Zhongwen were born in the same year, Changqian a month ahead; the clan nicknamed them Big Two and Little Two.

literal: In youth he and Wang Yanji of Taiyuan were both Editorial Assistants, supervising the collation of books.
idiomatic: As a young man he and Wang Yanji of Taiyuan served together as Editorial Assistants overseeing the collation of texts.

literal: Later he was Sima of Qingzhou.
idiomatic: He later became Sima of Qingzhou.

literal: When rebels besieged the city for two hundred days Changqian never laid down his brush; in all consultations he copied more than eight thousand sheets—astronomy, calendars, medicine, divination, wind horns, bird speech—there was nothing he did not master.
idiomatic: Rebels held the city two hundred days; Changqian never stopped writing, copying eight thousand sheets by hand in counsel—astronomy, calendrics, medicine, omens, wind lore, bird calls, all of it open to him.

literal: In his later years he was somewhat harmed by wine.
idiomatic: In later years wine took its toll.

literal: He was moved to Counsellor of the Masters of Writing, edited the Imperial Diary, and was given the added title Grand Master of Splendorous Light.
idiomatic: He rose to Counsellor of the Masters of Writing, kept the Imperial Diary, and was given the Splendorous Light grade.

literal: Later he was also Token Attendant Cavalier on a mission to Liang.
idiomatic: He later served as Token Attendant Cavalier on an embassy to Liang.

literal: Before leaving he told people, "My calamity lies in Wu lands; my taboo is the you year—I fear I shall not escape."
idiomatic: Before he set out he said, "My doom is in Wu country; my unlucky year is you—I may not return."

literal: On his return, before he had crossed the border, he died.
idiomatic: He died on the homeward road before he re-entered the realm.

literal: He was twenty-eight.
idiomatic: He was twenty-eight.

literal: He was posthumously made Governor of Southern Qing.
idiomatic: Posthumously he was made Governor of Southern Qing.

literal: Cheng's elder brother Yuan.
idiomatic: Cheng's elder brother was Yuan.

literal: Yuan, courtesy name Ningzu, was also famed in his time.
idiomatic: Yuan, style Ningzu, was likewise celebrated in his day.

literal: He was Left Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing under Murong Chui and Governor of Fan Yang and Changli.
idiomatic: Under Murong Chui he was Left Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing and Governor of Fan Yang and Changli.

literal: Yuan's great-grandson Yanshou was chief clerk of Jizhou.
idiomatic: Yuan's great-grandson Yanshou was chief clerk of Jizhou.

literal: Light with wealth and fond of giving, he won great praise in his district.
idiomatic: He spent freely and gave freely, and his neighborhood spoke well of him.

literal: Yanshou's son Longzong was plain and brotherly; his mourning was famed for filial piety.
idiomatic: Yanshou's son Longzong was open and devoted to his brothers; his filial mourning was widely praised.

literal: He held the governorships of Lanling and Yan.
idiomatic: He governed Lanling and Yan.

literal: He treated others with humaneness and trust, and was cautious to the point of sincerity; therefore he was valued in his time.
idiomatic: Humane and trustworthy, scrupulous to sincerity itself, he was held in esteem.

literal: When he died he was posthumously made Governor of Qi, with the posthumous name Filial.
idiomatic: At his death he was posthumously Governor of Qi, posthumous name Filial.

literal: His son Jingbao was Attendant in the Yitong office of Jizhou.
idiomatic: His son Jingbao was Attendant in the Jizhou Yitong office.

literal: He died and was posthumously made Governor of Ji.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made Governor of Ji.

literal: Jingbao's son Ziheng was Governor of Lu and died young.
idiomatic: Jingbao's son Ziheng was Governor of Lu and died early.

literal: Ziheng's brother's sons Zi'an and Zisheng, in the Wuding era, were executed in connection with the affair of Lian Yuanjin.
idiomatic: Ziheng's brother's sons Zi'an and Zisheng were put to death in the Wuding era in the Lian Yuanjin affair.

literal: A clansman of Cheng's, Mo, courtesy name Sifan, was descended from Yan's elder brother Ba.
idiomatic: Cheng's kinsman Mo, style Sifan, came down from Yan's elder brother Ba.

literal: His father Zun was Chamberlain for the Household under Murong Chui.
idiomatic: His father Zun had been Chamberlain for the Household under Murong Chui.

literal: Mo served Song as Governor of Rongyang.
idiomatic: Mo served the Song as Governor of Rongyang.

literal: In the Shenjuan era he pacified Pingtai and surrendered; afterward he was granted the barony of Wucheng.
idiomatic: In Shenjuan he pacified Pingtai and submitted; later he was enfeoffed as Baron of Wucheng.

literal: Mo was an elder of grave and sincere bearing who did not pursue glory or profit; though Cui Hao slighted him, he would not bend to Hao.
idiomatic: Mo was a man of weight and integrity who shunned advancement; Cui Hao despised him, yet he would not yield.

literal: He was close to Cui Yi and they came and went like one family.
idiomatic: He and Cui Yi were intimate, their households like one.

literal: At first, while Mo was in the south, his wife Lady Zhang had two sons, Zhongzhi and Jirou.
idiomatic: When Mo was still in the south, Lady Zhang bore him Zhongzhi and Jirou.

literal: When Mo reached the capital he was given Lady Jin as wife, and she bore Youdu.
idiomatic: At the capital he was given Lady Jin, who bore Youdu.

literal: Zhongzhi and the others, because their father was far away, gathered goods and plotted to ransom him home.
idiomatic: Zhongzhi and his brothers, their father lost in the north, pooled wealth to buy his return.

literal: Their mother Zhang said, "Your father's mind is irresolute in its aims—he surely cannot come."
idiomatic: Lady Zhang said, "Your father's resolve is weak—he will never come back."

literal: When the travelers brought the bribe to the capital, Mo indeed thought of Youdu and the others, and pointing to the travelers said, "How can I bear to abandon these children and let them suffer punishment?"
idiomatic: The envoys reached the capital with their price; Mo's heart turned to Youdu and the rest, and he told them, "How could I leave these boys to face torment?"

literal: "I shall obtain one man for you so that his name and rank do not fall below mine."
idiomatic: "I will give you a man whose standing will not dim mine."

literal: He then handed over Shen Mo, who was Governor of Dongjun in Song.
idiomatic: And he surrendered Shen Mo, Governor of Dongjun under Song.

literal: In the Shen
idiomatic: In the Shen

literal: juan era he was seized, given a wife, and had a son, Lingdu.
idiomatic: juan period he was taken, given a wife, and fathered Lingdu.

literal: When Shen Mo heard of this he abandoned wife and children and fled back beyond the Yangtze.
idiomatic: Shen Mo, hearing of it, cast off wife and children and fled south of the river.

literal: Lingdu was punished and made a gate eunuch.
idiomatic: Lingdu was sentenced and castrated as a palace gatekeeper.

literal: At first, in the last years of Zhijun, Mo's elder brother Xie's son Xieli was Governor of Lu in Song and surrendered the commandery.
idiomatic: Earlier, at the end of Zhijun, Mo's elder brother Xie's son Xieli, Governor of Lu under Song, surrendered his commandery.
